rv.q: Dwan climbs it, in every sense... a triumph for Lisa Dwan and Joe Murphy, her co-director.

Although fans of Beckett will revel in the opportunity to lose themselves in this kaleidoscopic maze of words, I'm not convinced that the 1,000-seat Old Vic is the right space for this feast of talkative intensity.
It's often very impressive. But I really didn't enjoy it at all that much.
It is always compelling, but the text is dense and elliptical, giving voice to a lost soul, battling nothingness, surrounded by the din of other phantoms, other ghosts.
The rest of us, and that’s most of us, coughed during much of the show and emerged in a state of shocked relief.
A new performance or, even more excitingly in this case, a new work, brings an intellectual and emotional ferocity that is entirely fresh, wholly demanding and completely enthralling.
It’s impossible to imagine these rendered better, such is the arch and shudder, the range and plangency of Dwon’s delivery.

cn.t: Dwan delivers an extraordinary, demanding performance of Beckett's adapted prose pieces, earning widespread praise for her interpretive skills, though the enigmatic, unperformed texts prove polarizing—mesmerizing some, exhausting others.
